_about: Pathway edges baked from Airtable Relations (single source of truth since 2026-09-30). Generated by relations_bake.py via Airtable REST (sync_relations.py). Do not edit by hand.

edges.mech: Unphosphorylated 4E-BP1 clamps onto eIF4E and stops it assembling the cap-binding complex. mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 to release that grip - so the brake on translation is released, not the accelerator pressed.
edges.mech_beginner: Untagged 4E-BP1 clamps onto eIF4E and blocks it; mTORC1 tags 4E-BP1 to make it let go – releasing a brake, not pressing an accelerator.

edges.mech: Keeping 4E-BP active extends lifespan under dietary restriction in flies, by enhancing mitochondrial activity. One of the few places where a single downstream node, not the whole pathway, carries the lifespan effect.
edges.ctx: Fly only, and only under dietary restriction - the effect was not seen on a full diet.
edges.note: Boundary condition matters more than the headline here.
edges.mech_beginner: Keeping 4E-BP switched on extends lifespan in fruit flies on a restricted diet, by protecting their mitochondria.

edges.mech: In mammalian cells (MOR2013) 4E-BPs repress translation of nucleus-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs, so mTORC1 raises mitochondrial output by inhibiting them; this arm is less rapamycin-sensitive than the S6K arm. In flies on dietary restriction (ZID2009) upregulated 4E-BP instead enhances translation of mitochondrial respiratory mRNAs. The sign depends on organism and nutrient state, so it is drawn as conditional.
edges.ctx: Scope: mammalian cells, MOR2013. The sign holds where 4E-BP represses translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs (TFAM, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins), which is why this branch survives rapamycin better than the S6K arm. It does NOT hold universally across species and nutrient states: in Drosophila under dietary restriction, ZID2009 reports that 4E-BP ENHANCES mitochondrial activity, and that this is how it extends lifespan. Treat the mammalian-cell direction as scoped, not general.
edges.note: ZID2009 is recorded as conflicting evidence on this edge (moved out of the supporting list on 2026-08-30): its own title says 4E-BP ENHANCES mitochondrial activity under dietary restriction in flies, which is the opposite sign to this mammalian-cell edge.
edges.mech_beginner: The 4E-BP branch helps set how many mitochondrial proteins get built. In mammalian cells it holds them back; in fruit flies on a restricted diet it boosts them, so the direction depends on the organism and the diet.

edges.mech: Akt phosphorylates PRAS40, which then gets sequestered away from mTORC1 - a second, parallel way insulin lifts a brake.
edges.mech_beginner: Akt tags PRAS40, which then gets pulled away from mTORC1 – a second way insulin releases a brake.

edges.mech: Akt phosphorylates TSC2, disabling the complex. Growth-factor signalling works by removing a brake, not by pressing an accelerator.
edges.mech_beginner: Akt tags TSC2 to disable it. Growth signals work by releasing a brake, not by pressing a gas pedal.

edges.mech: AMPK can promote the clearance of damaged mitochondria, in part by phosphorylating ULK1: cells whose ULK1 cannot be phosphorylated by AMPK show defective mitophagy under starvation. How much AMPK contributes depends on the cell type and on the kind of energy stress.
edges.ctx: Two studies of different kinds: EGA2010 (cells and C. elegans, AMPK-site mutant of ULK1) and ZHU2026 (mouse toxicology model, where LKB1/AMPK loss also went with mitochondrial DNA leakage and liver inflammation; that downstream link is shown only there). The upstream step is disputed: Park, Lee and Kim (Nat Commun 2023, PMID 37225695, outside this corpus) report that under energy stress AMPK restrains ULK1 activation; see AMPK-ULK1.
edges.mech_beginner: The cell's energy sensor can help clear out damaged mitochondria, partly by switching on an autophagy starter kinase. How much it matters depends on the cell and on the kind of stress.

edges.mech: AMPK also hits mTORC1 directly by phosphorylating Raptor, imposing a metabolic checkpoint independent of TSC.
edges.mech_beginner: AMPK also hits mTORC1 directly, adding a second, energy-based checkpoint on top of TSC.
edges.context: The Raptor arm is the TSC2-independent route, which is why it is measurable in TSC-null cells. Its relative contribution versus the TSC2 arm varies by cell type and by how deep the energy stress is.

edges.mech: When energy runs low, AMPK phosphorylates TSC2 and strengthens the brake on Rheb.
edges.mech_beginner: When energy is low, AMPK tags TSC2 and makes the brake on Rheb stronger.
edges.context: Relative weight of this arm is cell-type dependent. AMPK reaches mTORC1 two ways – activating TSC2 and directly phosphorylating Raptor – and TSC2-null cells still suppress mTORC1 under energy stress, so the TSC2 arm is not universally the dominant one. Which arm carries the signal depends on TSC status, LKB1 status and the severity and duration of the energy stress.

edges.mech: AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 at sites distinct from mTORC1's inhibitory S757 site. The classic reading is that low energy therefore switches autophagy on directly, not only by releasing the mTORC1 brake; that reading is now disputed (see boundary).
edges.ctx: Contested direction. EGA2010 and KIM2011 report activating phosphorylation. Park, Lee and Kim (Nat Commun 2023, PMID 37225695, outside this corpus) report that under glucose starvation and mitochondrial energy stress AMPK inhibits ULK1 activation and autophagy induction while protecting the ULK1 machinery from degradation. Which effect dominates appears to depend on the kind and depth of the energy stress.
edges.note: Two opposing inputs land on the same protein: this is where the pathway does arithmetic, not just relay.
edges.mech_beginner: AMPK also tags ULK1 directly. The long-standing view is that this switches cleanup on; newer work suggests that during a sharp energy crisis AMPK instead holds ULK1 back while protecting it, so the direction is now debated.

edges.mech: Cytosolic arginine binds CASTOR1 and breaks its grip on GATOR2 - the same trick as leucine/Sestrin2, but for a different amino acid.
edges.mech_beginner: Arginine sticks to CASTOR1 the same way leucine sticks to Sestrin2 – the same trick, for a different amino acid.

edges.mech: Arginine-free CASTOR1 binds GATOR2 and inhibits it, so the pathway stays off until arginine is available.
edges.mech_beginner: Without arginine, CASTOR1 holds onto GATOR2 and keeps the pathway switched off.

edges.mech: DEPTOR sits on mTOR and damps both complexes; myeloma cells overexpress it and depend on that damping.
edges.mech_beginner: DEPTOR sits on mTOR and dampens both complexes; some cancer cells (myeloma) make extra DEPTOR and come to depend on that damping.

edges.mech: Free eIF4E recruits the ribosome to the mRNA cap. This is the step that actually turns a growth signal into new protein.
edges.note: Not every mRNA is equally sensitive - HSI2012 shows a specific translational program, not a uniform increase.
edges.mech_beginner: Freed eIF4E brings the ribosome to the mRNA – the step that actually turns a growth signal into new protein.

edges.mech: ERK phosphorylates TSC2 and inactivates the TSC complex, so Ras-MAPK growth signalling converges on the same brake that Akt releases. This is the third upstream arm alongside PI3K/Akt and AMPK, and clinically it is a route to mTORC1 activation that PI3K inhibitors do not close.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus; Roux 2004 describes the parallel RSK arm and is not yet held.
edges.note: Added 2026-07-29. The graph previously had no MAPK input to mTORC1 at all.
edges.mech_beginner: A separate growth pathway also disables the TSC brake – a third route into mTORC1 that drugs blocking only PI3K/Akt can't shut down.

edges.mech: BOLERO-2: adding everolimus to hormone therapy roughly doubled progression-free survival in hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer.
edges.ctx: Progression-free survival, in combination with exemestane - overall survival was not significantly improved.
edges.note: Say PFS, not survival. The distinction is the whole argument of this Atlas.
edges.mech_beginner: Adding everolimus to hormone therapy roughly doubled the time before certain advanced breast cancers got worse.

edges.mech: Dose and schedule set the direction here, not the target. Intermittent low-dose everolimus improved influenza vaccine responses in older adults (MAN2014), while continuous transplant-level dosing of the same drug class is immunosuppressive. A larger phase 3 trial of a different mTOR inhibitor, RTB101 (an ATP-competitive PI3K/mTOR inhibitor), did not reduce respiratory illness (MAN2021), although it still switched on antiviral genes. The edge carries a conditional sign because the supported claim is regimen-specific rather than a net benefit to immune function.
edges.ctx: Dose-dependent and duration-dependent: this is not the immunosuppressive regimen. The corpus supports an improved vaccine response under one regimen, not improved immune function in general. MAN2021 is recorded as conflicting rather than supporting because it tested RTB101, a different drug, not everolimus.
edges.note: THE dose-dependence case study, and a genuine apparent contradiction with the drug's immunosuppressant label. Prime Contradiction Engine seed.
edges.mech_beginner: At a low, occasional dose, an mTOR-blocking drug helped older people respond better to a flu vaccine. At the high continuous dose used after transplants, mTOR inhibitors damp the immune system down. A larger phase 3 trial of a DIFFERENT mTOR inhibitor (RTB101, which blocks the kinase itself rather than working like rapamycin) found no reduction in respiratory illness – so what this arrow means depends on the dose, the schedule and the drug.
edges.teach: The one edge in this map whose sign is conditional. 'mTOR inhibition suppresses immunity' and 'low intermittent dosing improves the vaccine response of the old' are both supported, under different regimens, so a single activating arrow would be false in one of them. Dose and schedule belong to the claim here, not to the methods section.
edges.context: Direction depends on dose and schedule. Transplant-level dosing is immunosuppressive; intermittent low dosing improved vaccine responses in older adults. Treating this as one effect with one sign is the error.

edges.mech: EXIST-2 tested everolimus against renal angiomyolipoma in patients with tuberous sclerosis or sporadic LAM, and shrank those lesions by >=50% in 42% versus 0% on placebo.
edges.ctx: Scope: the endpoint was the kidney lesion, not LAM lung disease, which is why this arrow lands on the angiomyolipoma and not on LAM. The evidence that mTOR inhibition treats the lung disease itself is the MILES trial with sirolimus - see the RAPA-LAM edge.
edges.note: Rescoped 2026-07-29: this edge previously read as though everolimus had been shown to treat LAM.
edges.mech_beginner: In another trial, everolimus shrank kidney growths in patients with tuberous sclerosis or a related lung disease, working in 42% of patients versus 0% on placebo.

edges.mech: Everolimus is rapamycin with a solubilising side chain - same FKBP12 mechanism, better oral pharmacokinetics. It is the molecule that carried this pathway into routine clinical use.
edges.note: Six trials behind one arrow. They establish the clinical effect of the drug; the allosteric mechanism itself rests on the rapamycin biochemistry.
edges.mech_beginner: Everolimus is rapamycin with a small chemical tweak that makes it easier to take as a pill – same mechanism, better drug.

edges.mech: RADIANT-3: progression-free survival more than doubled in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.
edges.mech_beginner: In a trial, everolimus more than doubled the time before advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours got worse.

edges.mech: RECORD-1: everolimus roughly doubled progression-free survival after other targeted therapy failed.
edges.ctx: Second-line setting, after VEGF-targeted therapy - not first-line.
edges.mech_beginner: In a clinical trial, everolimus roughly doubled the time before advanced kidney cancer got worse, after other treatments had stopped working.

edges.mech: EXIST trials: everolimus shrank the brain tumours (SEGA) and kidney lesions of tuberous sclerosis - treating the pathway the mutation switches on, rather than a downstream symptom. The gene defect itself remains.
edges.ctx: Lesions regrow when the drug is stopped - this is suppression, not cure.
edges.note: The purest case in the Atlas: known gene, known pathway, matched drug, randomised evidence.
edges.mech_beginner: In patients with the genetic disease tuberous sclerosis, everolimus shrank both brain and kidney tumours. It works one step downstream of the mutation: it replaces the brake the mutation removed, so the tumours shrink while the drug is given and regrow when it stops. The mutation itself is untouched.

edges.mech: Only when it is carrying rapamycin, FKBP12 docks on the FRB domain next to mTOR's active site. The FKBP12-rapamycin complex, not FKBP12 alone, is what blocks access for some substrates but not all; FKBP12 without the drug does not inhibit mTORC1. The inhibitory arrow is drawn from rapamycin (RAPA-MTORC1).
edges.mech_beginner: Only when it carries rapamycin does FKBP12 dock on mTORC1; the pair then blocks some, but not all, of what mTORC1 does. FKBP12 on its own does nothing to mTORC1.
edges.teach: Partial, not complete. The FKBP12–rapamycin complex occludes the substrate channel, so S6K1 phosphorylation collapses while 4E-BP1 phosphorylation persists. This was a main motivation for developing ATP-competitive inhibitors.

edges.mech: FLCN-FNIP is the GAP for the other half of the Rag dimer (RagC/D). Only when both halves are in the right nucleotide state can the dimer hold mTORC1. Crucially this arm is SUBSTRATE-SPECIFIC: it gates TFEB and TFE3 phosphorylation, while canonical outputs like S6K1 and 4E-BP1 carry on without it.
edges.ctx: The substrate selectivity is why Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is driven by constitutive nuclear TFEB/TFE3 rather than by blanket mTORC1 hyperactivation (NAP2020).
edges.mech_beginner: FLCN flips the other half of the Rag pair into its working shape – but it only changes one specific output (TFEB), not the whole pathway.
edges.teach: Positive regulator of the RagC/D arm, despite being a tumour suppressor. It licenses mTORC1 to phosphorylate TFEB specifically – substrate choice, not overall activity.

edges.mech: GATOR1 acts as a GAP: it forces RagA/B to hydrolyse GTP, flipping the Rag heterodimer into the inactive shape that cannot hold mTORC1.
edges.mech_beginner: GATOR1 forces the Rag proteins into their "off" shape, so they can no longer hold onto mTORC1.

edges.mech: Released GATOR2 suppresses GATOR1 - a double negative. Two brakes in series is why the sensors can flip mTORC1 on so sharply.
edges.ctx: The epistasis is solid. VAL2022 resolved GATOR2's architecture by cryo-EM - a 1.1 MDa cage - and mapped where the sensors dock, but exactly how GATOR2 suppresses GATOR1's GAP activity is still not settled.
edges.note: Good candidate for a 'mechanism gap' flag - textbook arrow, thin mechanistic evidence.
edges.mech_beginner: GATOR2 shuts down GATOR1 – a brake acting on another brake. That double-negative is part of why the switch flips on so sharply, though exactly how isn't fully worked out yet.
edges.teach: Everyone agrees this inhibition happens; nobody has fully resolved how. Kept visible as an honest hole in a canonical pathway.

edges.mech: Glutamine burned through glutaminolysis raises alpha-ketoglutarate, which promotes RagB GTP loading and mTORC1 translocation to the lysosome. This edge asserts the Rag-dependent route only.
edges.ctx: Cell-type dependent, and deliberately narrow: the separate claim that glutamine can reach mTORC1 without the Rags is carried by its own edge rather than folded in here.
edges.note: Split from the Rag-independent claim on 2026-09-13 after external review: one edge was asserting a Rag-dependent mechanism and describing a Rag-independent one in the same sentence.
edges.mech_beginner: Glutamine can switch on mTORC1 partly just by being burned for fuel: burning it makes a molecule that helps the Rag proteins pull mTORC1 to the lysosome.

edges.mech: Stabilised Grb10 damps insulin/IGF-1 receptor signalling. This is one of two feedback arms behind the paradox that blocking mTORC1 raises Akt activity; the other is the S6K1-IRS-1 loop.
edges.note: ORE2006 and ROD2011 were removed from this edge on 2026-09-21: neither measured Grb10. ORE2006 belongs to the S6K1-IRS-1 arm and ROD2011 shows relief of receptor tyrosine kinase feedback in general.
edges.mech_beginner: Grb10 dampens insulin/IGF-1 signalling – which is why blocking mTOR can paradoxically make Akt more active.

edges.mech: Low oxygen induces REDD1 transcriptionally over hours, slower than AMPK. REDD1 protein is short-lived, so the signal lasts only as long as hypoxia keeps the gene switched on.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus.
edges.note: Thin - one supporting study.
edges.mech_beginner: Low oxygen quickly switches on the gene for REDD1 – slower to kick in than AMPK, but longer-lasting.

edges.mech: Insulin and IGF-1 dock on their receptor, which recruits IRS proteins and switches on PI3K to make the lipid messenger PIP3.
edges.mech_beginner: Insulin and IGF-1 latch onto their receptor and switch on PI3K, which builds a signalling lipid.

edges.mech: IRS proteins are the adaptors that carry the signal from the insulin/IGF-1 receptor to PI3K. Deplete them and the receptor is still there but the wire is cut.
edges.mech_beginner: IRS proteins carry the signal from the insulin receptor to PI3K; without them, the receptor is still there but the wire connecting it is cut.

edges.mech: The integrated stress response switches on Salr, a growth inhibitor - a route into mTORC1 that bypasses TSC and AMPK entirely.
edges.ctx: Fly only, and newly reported.
edges.note: Thin and species-limited, but it is a genuinely different input route - worth showing as such.
edges.mech_beginner: The cell's stress-response system switches on a growth-blocking gene – a route to shutting down mTORC1 that skips right past TSC and AMPK.

edges.mech: KICSTOR is the dock that holds GATOR1 on the lysosomal surface. Without it, GATOR1 cannot reach its target and nutrient control of mTORC1 is lost.
edges.mech_beginner: KICSTOR works like a docking clamp that holds GATOR1 in place on the lysosome; without it, GATOR1 can't reach its target.

edges.mech: In this model LARS acts as a GAP for RagD, doing for the RagC/D half what FLCN does - an alternative route from leucine to the Rags.
edges.ctx: Human cell biochemistry only, and cell-type dependence was never mapped. The reaction it claims - GAP activity on the RagC/D half - is the same reaction this Atlas assigns to FLCN, and the two assignments have never been reconciled head-to-head. Read together with LEU-LARS: if the upstream leucine-sensing claim does not hold, this edge loses its input.
edges.note: See LEU-LARS.
edges.mech_beginner: In that model, this enzyme flips the other Rag protein into its working shape – an alternative route from leucine to the Rags.

edges.mech: A competing model: the enzyme that loads leucine onto tRNA doubles as the leucine sensor, binding free leucine directly.
edges.ctx: Proposed before the Sestrin2 model and never cleanly reconciled with it.
edges.note: CONTESTED with LEU-SESN2. Two published leucine sensors, both from strong labs, never resolved head-to-head. Prime Contradiction Engine seed.
edges.mech_beginner: One competing idea: the enzyme that loads leucine onto its transport molecule for protein-building doubles as the leucine sensor.

edges.mech: Leucine binds a pocket inside Sestrin2 with roughly 20 uM affinity - close to the concentration at which cells actually feel leucine coming and going. The bound sensor can no longer hold GATOR2, so leucine effectively switches the brake off.
edges.ctx: Affinity was measured in vitro; whether the same 20 uM setpoint holds in tissues with different leucine transport is untested.
edges.mech_beginner: Leucine sticks to a pocket inside Sestrin2 and makes it let go of the next protein in line – that's how the cell notices leucine is around.

edges.mech: LKB1 is the kinase that primes AMPK, phosphorylating AMPK-alpha directly on Thr172; without it the whole energy-stress arm is deaf.
edges.ctx: Canonical step, established in LKB1-null cells and in vitro kinase assays (SHW2004). Coded M – molecular – because that is what the supporting evidence is: cell and in vitro biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.
edges.note: Until 2026-07-29 this edge was supported only by ZHU2026, a trichloroethylene liver-injury study that is consistent with the step but was not designed to establish it. Re-cited to Shaw 2004.
edges.mech_beginner: LKB1 is the kinase that switches AMPK on in the first place; without it, the whole low-energy alarm system goes silent.

edges.mech: In the canonical nutrient-dependent route, mTORC1 has to reach the lysosomal surface to be switched on, because that is where Rheb is waiting. Force it elsewhere and amino acids stop mattering. The requirement is stated for this route, not for every pool of mTOR in the cell.
edges.ctx: Scoped to amino-acid-driven activation. Live BRET imaging in this corpus (BOU2020) resolves mTOR activity in the cytosol, at the lysosome, in the nucleus and near mitochondria, so mTOR signalling is measurably not one pool. This map draws the lysosomal route and keeps the other localisations declared as open rather than asserting there are none. FER2024 refines this further: lysosomal mTORC1 (fed by local lysosomal proteolysis) and cytoplasmic mTORC1 (fed by exogenous amino acids) phosphorylate distinct downstream substrates — the lysosome is required for one regulatory sub-pool of mTORC1, not for all of it.
edges.mech_beginner: In the amino-acid route, mTORC1 only works while it's sitting on the lysosome, because that is where its activator waits – move it somewhere else and amino acids stop being able to reach it.
edges.teach: A requirement, not a signal. The lysosome contributes a location. Read it as the canonical amino-acid route rather than a universal rule for mTOR: BOU2020 resolves mTOR activity in several compartments, and the map declares those localisations as open instead of asserting they do not exist.

edges.mech: Metformin shifts the cell's energy balance and AMPK switches on - the route it is usually credited to, and why it keeps appearing next to rapamycin in longevity discussions.
edges.ctx: How much of metformin's effect actually runs through AMPK is disputed: it still suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis in AMPK-null and LKB1-null mouse liver (FOR2010) and still inhibits mTORC1 in AMPK-null cells (KAL2010). See the parallel METFORMIN-MTORC1 edge.
edges.mech_beginner: Metformin shifts the cell's energy balance and switches AMPK on – its best-known route to affecting this pathway.

edges.mech: Metformin also inhibits mTORC1 WITHOUT going through AMPK: the effect survives in AMPK-null and TSC1/2-null cells and instead requires the Rag GTPases. This is the arm usually left out of the 'metformin works via AMPK' summary.
edges.ctx: Runs in parallel with METFORMIN-AMPK, not instead of it. The relative weight of the two routes in humans is unresolved.
edges.note: FOR2010 was removed from this edge on 2026-09-21: it measured hepatic gluconeogenesis and never read out mTORC1. It remains correctly cited in the boundary of METFORMIN-AMPK.
edges.mech_beginner: Metformin can also block mTORC1 through a completely separate route that doesn't need AMPK at all – a route often left out of the simple "metformin works via AMPK" story.
edges.context: Dose is the whole argument. Concentrations used in cell culture are typically far above plasma levels achieved at clinical doses, so in vitro mechanism may not describe what metformin does in a patient.

edges.mech: mLST8 is dispensable for mTORC1 in vivo but essential for mTORC2 - a rare clean genetic separation of the two complexes.
edges.note: The cleanest genetic argument that the two complexes are truly separate machines.
edges.mech_beginner: This protein isn't needed for mTORC1 in a living animal, but mTORC2 can't work without it – a clean genetic way to tell the two complexes apart.

edges.mech: mTORC2 is built around the same mTOR kinase as mTORC1 - the partner subunits, not the catalytic core, are what make the two complexes different.
edges.note: Three independent structures - unusually well supported for this corpus.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC2 is built from the very same mTOR enzyme as mTORC1 – it's the partner proteins around it that make the two complexes different.

edges.mech: mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1, which lets go of eIF4E and frees cap-dependent translation. Rapamycin blocks this arm only partially - the origin of the whole 'rapamycin-resistant output' problem.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 tags 4E-BP1 so it lets go of another protein, freeing up protein-building – but the standard drug (rapamycin) only partly blocks this step.
edges.teach: The sign is on 4E-BP1's repressor function: mTORC1 phosphorylates it, which stops it repressing eIF4E. Phosphorylation is not the same as inhibition – here it happens to be.

edges.mech: mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises Grb10 - the start of a feedback loop that talks back to the insulin receptor.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 stabilises Grb10, kicking off a feedback loop that talks back to the insulin receptor.

edges.mech: Lowering mTORC1 activity extends lifespan across yeast, worms, flies and mice - one of the most conserved interventions in ageing biology, alongside dietary restriction.
edges.ctx: No human hard-endpoint evidence. This is the Atlas's flagged 'human endpoint desert'.
edges.note: Links to ATLAS_FINDINGS human-endpoint desert.
edges.mech_beginner: Turning mTORC1 down extends lifespan in yeast, worms, flies and mice – one of the most universal anti-ageing effects known.
edges.context: Strongly modified by sex, strain, diet and the age at which inhibition starts. Effect direction is reproducible; effect size is not transferable between models.

edges.mech: A second feedback arm: inhibiting mTORC1 releases a PI3K-dependent brake and MAPK signalling goes up. Together with S6K1-IRS1 this is why single-agent mTOR inhibition tends to be met by compensatory growth signalling.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus.
edges.note: CAR2008 was already in the corpus but carried no edge until 2026-07-29.
edges.mech_beginner: Blocking mTORC1 can backfire by releasing a brake on a different growth pathway (MAPK) – one reason mTOR-blocking drugs alone often aren't enough.
edges.teach: The second feedback arm. mTORC1 inhibition activates ERK PI3K-dependently, which is the rationale for combined mTOR/MEK strategies.

edges.mech: mTORC1 raises mitochondrial output two ways: through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcription complex, and by relieving 4E-BP so mitochondrial proteins get translated.
edges.ctx: Shown in cultured cells and skeletal muscle (CUN2007) and mammalian cell lines (MOR2013). One organismal result points the other way: adipose-specific Raptor deletion raised mitochondrial respiration (POL2008), see MTORC1-OXPHOS.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 boosts the cell's mitochondria – its power plants – two ways at once: through a gene-activating complex, and by freeing up 4E-BP.

edges.mech: mTORC1 couples nucleotide supply to demand - it turns on purine synthesis through the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate cycle so a dividing cell can actually copy its DNA.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 turns on the machinery for building DNA/RNA building blocks, so a growing cell can actually copy its DNA.

edges.mech: Blocking mTOR reversed Akt-driven pre-cancerous prostate lesions in mice, showing the growth was mTORC1-dependent and reversible.
edges.ctx: Scope: the lesion was prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a pre-cancerous stage, driven by transgenic human AKT1 in mice, and the drug (RAD001) inhibits mTORC1 allosterically. Mouse only in this corpus. Not a demonstration in established prostate cancer.
edges.note: The arrow means mTORC1 inhibition reversed a pre-cancerous prostate lesion in a mouse model. It is not a claim that mTORC1 drives established prostate cancer.
edges.mech_beginner: Blocking mTOR reversed early, pre-cancerous prostate changes in mice caused by an overactive growth signal.

edges.mech: Renal cancers frequently carry lesions that leave mTORC1 constitutively active - which is why this tissue responds to mTOR inhibitors at all, and why an exceptional responder could be traced to TSC1 loss.
edges.ctx: Correlative plus one n-of-1 genomic case (IYE2012); not a demonstration that mTORC1 activation initiates RCC.
edges.note: Replaces TUMOR-RCC, which asserted 'Tumor growth activates RCC' - a category error, since RCC is an instance of tumour growth, not a downstream target.
edges.mech_beginner: Many kidney cancers carry mutations that leave mTORC1 stuck "on" – that's why this cancer type responds to mTOR-blocking drugs at all, though it doesn't prove mTORC1 causes the cancer.
edges.teach: Association, not demonstrated causation. Renal cancers often carry lesions that leave mTORC1 active; that is why the tissue responds to rapalogs, not proof that mTORC1 initiates the disease.

edges.mech: mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1, switching on the translation machinery. This is the classic rapamycin-sensitive output and the readout most papers actually measure.
edges.ctx: Caution: p-S6K is a proxy, not the phenotype. Many 'mTORC1 activity' claims rest on this single band.
edges.note: Worth flagging on the page: readout != outcome.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 switches on S6K1, which turns on the cell's protein-building machinery – the classic effect most studies of this drug class measure.
edges.context: Standard mTORC1 readout, but a readout is not the whole output. S6K1 phosphorylation is fully rapamycin-sensitive while 4E-BP1 is not, so 'mTORC1 activity' measured by S6K1 alone systematically overstates how much rapamycin inhibits mTORC1.

edges.mech: mTORC1 sustains the inflammatory secretory output of cells that are already senescent, by promoting IL1A translation. Inhibiting it quietens that output without reversing the proliferative arrest.
edges.ctx: Three studies, all in cells or a rat disease model. LAB2015 and NAR2011 measure the secretory output of cells that are already senescent (IL1A translation; IL-6/IL-8 production fuelled by mTOR at the TASCC). CHEN2026C (human disc cells, rat needle-puncture model) shows mTORC1 hyperactivation after TSC2 loss together with senescence and SASP, both blocked by rapamycin - a disease-model result, not a general demonstration that mTORC1 drives cells into senescence. That is why this arrow lands on the secretory programme and not on senescence itself.
edges.note: The arrow means mTORC1 sustains the secretory output (SASP) of senescent cells. Whether mTORC1 also pushes cells into senescence in the first place (geroconversion) is a separate and weaker claim that this edge does not make.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 keeps old, "senescent" cells pumping out inflammatory signals, and blocking it calms that output down without making those cells young again. Whether mTORC1 also helps push cells into senescence in the first place is a separate question this arrow does not answer.
edges.teach: The arrow points at the SASP node, not at Cellular senescence, because that is the claim the evidence supports: LAB2015 shows mTORC1 promoting IL1A translation in cells that are ALREADY arrested, and rapamycin suppressing the secretome while the arrest stays. Whether mTORC1 also pushes cells into senescence is a separate claim with weaker, context-bound support (CHEN2026C, a disc-degeneration model), and this arrow does not make it. Conflating SASP and senescence is the commonest misreading here.

edges.mech: mTORC1 drives the SREBP transcription factors, which turn on the genes for making fat and cholesterol - growth needs membrane, not just protein.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 switches on SREBP, the genes that build fat and cholesterol – a growing cell needs membrane material, not just protein.

edges.mech: Active mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB right on the lysosomal surface, trapping it in the cytoplasm. Switch mTORC1 off and TFEB walks into the nucleus.
edges.ctx: RagD specifically (more than RagC) promotes TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation via tighter LAMTOR binding — GOL2022 shows this is paralogue-specific, not a generic Rag-dimer property.
edges.note: Four independent studies - one of the best-supported output edges.
edges.mech_beginner: Active mTORC1 tags TFEB and traps it outside the nucleus; switch mTORC1 off and TFEB moves in.
edges.context: Substrate-selective. Depends on FLCN/FNIP RagC/D status, so mTORC1 can be active on S6K1 while not phosphorylating TFEB.

edges.mech: Hyperactive mTORC1 reprograms translation toward a specific set of pro-growth and pro-metastasis mRNAs (HSI2012, prostate models) and couples nucleotide synthesis to demand, creating a targetable vulnerability in TSC-deficient cells (VAL2017).
edges.ctx: Context-dependent: shown in genetically driven mouse tumour models and cancer cell lines with hyperactive mTORC1 (PTEN loss, TSC loss), not as a general property of tumours.
edges.note: The arrow means hyperactive mTORC1 promotes tumour growth where the pathway is already unleashed - PTEN-loss and TSC-loss backgrounds. It is not a claim that mTORC1 activity causes tumours generally, and normal mTORC1 signalling is not a tumour driver here.
edges.mech_beginner: Hyperactive mTORC1 pushes cells to build a specific set of growth- and spread-promoting proteins – the tumour becomes hooked on that programme.

edges.mech: Active mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 at an inhibitory site, holding autophagy shut while nutrients are plentiful.
edges.mech_beginner: Active mTORC1 tags ULK1 to hold it back, keeping the cell's self-cleanup process (autophagy) switched off while nutrients are plentiful.

edges.mech: One of the first functions assigned to mTORC2 was shaping the cell's skeleton. In yeast it was the original TOR2 phenotype; in mammalian cells it showed that the second complex is acutely rapamycin-insensitive.
edges.note: The two-complex model itself came from biochemistry (LOE2002, JAC2004, SAR2004).
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC2's first known job was shaping the cell's internal skeleton – noticed precisely because rapamycin didn't block it.

edges.mech: mTORC2 puts the second, activating phosphate on Akt (Ser473). This is the step rapamycin eventually breaks, and a major reason, in mice, that chronic rapamycin impairs glucose tolerance (LAM2012).
edges.note: Bridge edge between the growth-factor route and the rapamycin route.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC2 adds the final activating tag to Akt – the same step that long-term use of the drug rapamycin eventually disrupts. In mice, that disruption is a major reason long-term rapamycin raises blood sugar.
edges.context: S473 contribution to Akt output is substrate-dependent: some Akt substrates are strongly mTORC2-dependent, others barely.

edges.mech: Losing mTORC2 uncouples Akt from insulin signalling and produces glucose intolerance - and this is separable from the lifespan benefit.
edges.ctx: In mice, intermittent dosing largely spared glucose tolerance while keeping mTORC1 inhibition (ARR2015); not tested against this endpoint in humans.
edges.note: Feeds hypothesis H2 in Knowledge_Gaps.
edges.mech_beginner: Losing mTORC2 disconnects Akt from insulin signalling and can cause blood-sugar problems – a separate effect from any lifespan benefit.

edges.mech: In an mTOR-driven mouse liver model that progresses from steatosis to hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic mTORC2 promoted de novo fatty-acid, sphingolipid and cardiolipin synthesis, and blocking lipid synthesis prevented the tumours.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus, shown in one mouse liver tumour model (GUR2017) that progresses from steatosis to hepatocellular carcinoma. Mouse only - not tested in another species in this corpus. Not established as a general mTORC2 function outside that setting.
edges.note: The arrow means mTORC2 drove de novo lipid synthesis in one hepatic tumour model. It is not a claim that mTORC2 controls lipid synthesis generally, or in people.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC2 also drives fat-making, which is one of the ways it is thought to help tumours grow – shown in cells and mice, not measured in patients.

edges.mech: Prostate cancer driven by Pten loss needs mTORC2 to develop; normal prostate does not. A real therapeutic window, at least in mice.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus (GUE2009). Shown in Pten-null mouse prostate only: mTORC2 (Rictor) is required for tumours to develop in that genetic background, while normal prostate epithelium is not dependent on it. Mouse only - not tested in another species in this corpus, and not shown in human prostate cancer.
edges.note: The arrow means mTORC2 is required for Pten-loss-driven prostate cancer to develop in mice. It does not claim that mTORC2 causes prostate cancer, and it says nothing about human disease.
edges.mech_beginner: Prostate tumours caused by losing a specific tumour-suppressor gene (Pten) need mTORC2 to develop – normal prostate tissue doesn't, at least in mice.

edges.mech: SGK1 is a second mTORC2 substrate alongside Akt, and it carries some of the functions usually credited to Akt.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus.
edges.mech_beginner: SGK1 is a second target of mTORC2 alongside Akt, and it shares some of Akt's jobs.

edges.mech: PDCD4 blocks the eIF4A helicase, so mRNAs with structured 5' ends cannot be unwound and translated.
edges.ctx: SOURCING FLAG (2026-09-04): the mechanism stated here is correct and canonical, but no study currently in this corpus demonstrates it. Treat as an unsourced canonical step until Yang 2003 or Suzuki 2008 is added.
edges.mech_beginner: PDCD4 jams a helper enzyme so some mRNAs can't be unwound and read.

edges.mech: PIP3 pulls Akt to the membrane, where it gets phosphorylated and activated.
edges.mech_beginner: That lipid pulls Akt to the cell membrane, where it gets switched on.
edges.teach: Indirect on purpose: PI3K makes PIP3, and PIP3 recruits Akt. Recruitment then enables two separate phosphorylations. Three distinct events often drawn as one arrow.
edges.context: PIP3 recruits Akt; recruitment alone does not activate it. Full activation additionally needs PDK1 (T308) and mTORC2 (S473), so the strength of this link depends on the activity of both of those.

edges.mech: PIP3 made by PI3K binds SIN1 and releases its hold on the kinase site - so growth-factor signalling switches mTORC2 on, not only mTORC1.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus.
edges.note: Thin - one supporting study for a step drawn as canonical.
edges.mech_beginner: The same lipid signal that switches Akt on also switches mTORC2 on – so growth-factor signals hit both complexes.

edges.mech: Unphosphorylated PRAS40 sits in the substrate groove of mTORC1 and blocks it - a built-in plug.
edges.mech_beginner: Untagged PRAS40 sits inside mTORC1 and blocks it, like a built-in plug.

edges.mech: PTEN erases PIP3, undoing PI3K. Losing PTEN is one of the commonest ways a tumour leaves this whole axis switched on without an upstream signal.
edges.ctx: The cancer genetics here is mouse work (GUE2009). The biochemical step itself, PTEN dephosphorylating PIP3, has no dedicated paper in this corpus.
edges.note: MAJ2004 was removed from this edge on 2026-09-21: it used Akt-transgenic mice and never manipulated PTEN, so it could not support this step and should not have been setting the edge's tier and species.
edges.mech_beginner: PTEN erases the lipid signal that PI3K makes. Losing PTEN is one of the most common ways cancers keep this whole pathway switched on without any signal from outside.
edges.teach: PTEN does not touch the PI3K protein. It removes PI3K's product. Drawn as an inhibition arrow for readability – the mechanism is enzymatic reversal.
edges.context: The 'inhibits' label describes the net effect on signalling, not the enzyme itself: PTEN does not inhibit PI3K catalytically. It dephosphorylates PIP3, PI3K's lipid product, erasing the signal downstream of the enzyme rather than blocking PI3K's activity.

edges.mech: The active Rag dimer grabs Raptor and physically drags mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface. This is a relocation, not an activation - the kinase is moved to where its activator waits.
edges.ctx: Rag paralogues are not interchangeable: RagC/D sets substrate specificity downstream (RagD favors TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation via tighter LAMTOR binding, while both Rags are involved for non-lysosomal substrates like S6K), and RagA/B sets the response to amino acid withdrawal (RagB-expressing cells keep mTORC1 lysosomal and active even when starved) — GOL2022.
edges.note: The conceptual crux of the whole route: teach recruitment vs activation as two separate ideas.
edges.mech_beginner: The switched-on Rag proteins grab mTORC1 and drag it to the lysosome. This moves it into place; it doesn't turn it on by itself.
edges.teach: Recruitment, not activation. The Rags decide *where* mTORC1 is; they do not switch the kinase on. This is why, in the canonical model, amino acids on their own are not enough to drive growth.

edges.mech: Ragulator does two jobs on the Rags. It tethers the Rag heterodimer to the lysosomal surface, and it acts as an unusual exchange factor: first reported as a GEF for RagA/B (BAR2012), its exchange activity was later placed on RagC, where releasing GTP unlocks the inactive state (SHE2018B). Loading RagA with GTP is done by arginine-bound SLC38A9 (see SLC38A9-RAG).
edges.mech_beginner: Ragulator anchors the Rag proteins to the lysosome and also helps flip them into their "on" shape, together with a second protein, SLC38A9. Both jobs are shown in biochemical experiments.

edges.mech: Rapamycin is not an ordinary inhibitor: it first binds the small protein FKBP12, and only the two-part complex is the real drug.
edges.note: The molecular-glue concept - genuinely surprising to newcomers.
edges.mech_beginner: Rapamycin doesn't work alone – it first has to team up with a helper protein called FKBP12.

edges.mech: The MILES trial: sirolimus stabilised lung function (FEV1) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis while patients took it, and decline resumed after stopping. This - not the everolimus angiomyolipoma trial - is the evidence that mTOR inhibition treats LAM lung disease.
edges.ctx: Benefit is suppressive: lung function declined again after withdrawal.
edges.note: Added 2026-07-29. EVE-LAM previously carried this claim on a trial whose endpoint was renal angiomyolipoma.
edges.mech_beginner: In a clinical trial, rapamycin stabilised lung function in a rare lung disease while patients kept taking it – the decline came back once they stopped.

edges.mech: Rapamycin extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice even when started late in life - one of the most influential results in the geroscience arm of this Atlas.
edges.ctx: Mouse only. No human lifespan or healthspan endpoint exists; EVERLAST has no results yet. BIT2016 shows a non-continuous schedule can still extend post-treatment life expectancy, but the result is dose- and route-specific: in the 8 mg/kg/day intraperitoneal arm males gained +60% post-treatment life expectancy (p=0.02) while females showed no survival benefit (p=0.261) and a shift toward aggressive haematopoietic cancers (16/16 vs 6/12, p=0.002); in the same paper's 126 ppm dietary encapsulated-rapamycin arm survival rose significantly in BOTH sexes, with a Cox model finding no evidence that sex modified the treatment effect (p=0.904). Cite the arm, not just the paper. ARR2016: an intermittent regimen (2 mg/kg every 5 days) started as late as 20 months of age extended lifespan in female C57BL/6J mice; the abstract reports the effect in females only.
edges.note: ARR2015 was removed from this edge on 2026-07-29: that study measured side effects only and has no survival endpoint.
edges.mech_beginner: Rapamycin makes mice live longer, even when given late in life – the single biggest result behind the whole "this pathway and ageing" idea.

edges.mech: Rapamycin does not touch mTORC2 in the short term - but over days it traps free mTOR and prevents new mTORC2 from being assembled.
edges.ctx: Strictly time- and cell-type-dependent: absent acutely, present after prolonged exposure, and the sensitivity varies between cell lines. LAM2012 shows the same loss of mTORC2 signalling in mouse liver in vivo, so this is not a cell-culture-only phenomenon. Treating this edge as unconditional is a common error.
edges.note: THE key context-dependent edge. Should render dashed with an explicit 'chronic only' label.
edges.mech_beginner: Rapamycin doesn't touch mTORC2 right away, but over days it stops new mTORC2 from being built.

edges.mech: Raptor is the subunit that defines mTORC1 and presents substrates to the kinase.
edges.mech_beginner: Raptor is the piece that makes mTORC1 what it is, and hands it the targets it needs to act on.

edges.mech: REDD1 works through the TSC complex, not around it - hypoxia and growth factors therefore converge on the same brake.
edges.mech_beginner: REDD1 acts through the TSC brake, so low oxygen and low growth-factor signals end up hitting the very same switch.

edges.mech: GTP-loaded Rheb binds mTORC1 at the lysosome and physically re-shapes its active site into the working conformation.
edges.note: Convergence point: the amino-acid route delivers mTORC1 here, the growth-factor route delivers Rheb. Both required.
edges.mech_beginner: Switched-on Rheb docks onto mTORC1 and physically reshapes it into its working form – the actual "on" switch.
edges.teach: This is the activation step, and it only works on mTORC1 that the amino-acid arm has already brought to the lysosome. Everything the growth-factor arm does converges here.
edges.context: Rheb must be GTP-loaded and co-located with mTORC1. Rheb is also distributed across the ER and Golgi, and which pool supplies the activating Rheb is unresolved.

edges.mech: Rictor defines the second complex, mTORC2, which rapamycin does not block acutely.
edges.mech_beginner: Rictor is what makes the second complex, mTORC2, distinct – and rapamycin doesn't block it right away.

edges.mech: One of the pathway's major negative feedback loops, and the best studied. Sustained S6K1 activity, as in obesity and nutrient excess, phosphorylates IRS-1 and represses its expression, so the insulin receptor can no longer signal to PI3K. This is a major reason blocking mTORC1 paradoxically RAISES Akt activity (the Grb10 arm adds to it). Rapalog-associated insulin resistance runs mainly through a different route, disruption of mTORC2 (LAM2012, in mice).
edges.ctx: Established in cells and mouse genetics. The size of this arm's contribution to rapalog dysglycaemia in humans, relative to mTORC2 loss, has not been apportioned.
edges.note: Added 2026-07-29 after external review found this canonical loop missing from the graph.
edges.mech_beginner: This is one of the pathway's main self-limiting "off switches": strong, sustained S6K1 activity shuts down IRS-1, cutting the insulin signal off. That is how too much food can blunt the insulin signal. It also runs the other way: block mTOR and IRS-1 survives, so Akt can paradoxically become MORE active – which is why the insulin resistance seen on these drugs is blamed, on evidence from mice, on a different mechanism (loss of mTORC2), not on this loop.
edges.teach: One of the most clinically consequential feedback loops, and the direction matters twice over: active mTORC1 destroys IRS-1 (insulin resistance under nutrient excess), while blocking mTORC1 spares IRS-1 and reactivates PI3K/Akt. A large part of why rapalog monotherapy underperforms.

edges.mech: Deleting S6K1 extends median lifespan in FEMALE mice (+19% in SEL2009); the effect was not significant in males. It also protects against diet-induced obesity. Read the sex qualifier as part of the claim: this is the clearest evidence that one downstream branch, rather than mTORC1 as a whole, carries much of the ageing signal, and it is also the result whose qualifier is most often dropped in retelling.
edges.ctx: Female mice only in SEL2009 - the lifespan extension was not significant in males.
edges.note: Feeds the sex-dimorphism hypothesis H6 in Knowledge_Gaps.
edges.mech_beginner: Removing S6K1 makes FEMALE mice live longer (about a fifth longer) and resist obesity. In male mice the same change did not significantly extend life – that difference is part of the result, not a footnote. Still strong evidence that one branch, not the whole pathway, drives much of the ageing effect.
edges.teach: The Atlas's own H6 sex-dimorphism hypothesis starts here, and this is the result whose qualifier is lost in retelling most often. SEL2009's extension is female-specific; the male arm was not significant. An earlier external review found the qualifier stated in some places and dropped in others, which is why it now sits in the claim itself and not only in the boundary conditions.

edges.mech: S6K1 phosphorylates CAD, the enzyme that starts de novo pyrimidine synthesis - a direct line from growth signal to DNA building blocks.
edges.mech_beginner: S6K1 switches on an enzyme that starts building the raw materials for DNA – a direct line from growth signal to DNA parts.

edges.mech: S6K1 tags PDCD4 for destruction. PDCD4 is itself a translation inhibitor, so removing it is a second, parallel way mTORC1 lifts a brake on protein synthesis.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge in this corpus.
edges.note: Thin - one supporting study.
edges.mech_beginner: S6K1 marks PDCD4, itself a brake on protein-building, for destruction – a second way mTORC1 releases the brake.

edges.mech: Salr suppresses mTORC1-driven growth downstream of stress signalling.
edges.mech_beginner: This stress-induced protein suppresses mTORC1-driven growth once stress signalling turns it on.

edges.mech: S-adenosylmethionine, the cell's methyl-donor currency, binds SAMTOR and pulls it off GATOR1 - this is how methionine availability reaches mTORC1.
edges.ctx: Single-study edge. Needs independent replication before it is treated as established.
edges.note: Only one supporting study in the corpus - flag as thin.
edges.mech_beginner: SAM, a byproduct of methionine, binds SAMTOR and pulls it away from GATOR1 – the proposed way the cell senses how much methionine it has. Worked out in cells; whether this sensor is what matters in a whole animal has not been shown.

edges.mech: Methionine-starved SAMTOR binds the GATOR1-KICSTOR complex and helps it keep mTORC1 off.
edges.note: Only one supporting study in the corpus.
edges.mech_beginner: When methionine is low, SAMTOR teams up with GATOR1 to help keep mTORC1 switched off.

edges.mech: Losing Drosophila Sestrin produces fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle degeneration and cardiac malfunction, all prevented by inhibiting TOR or activating AMPK. Sestrin therefore limits age-associated pathology in the fly.
edges.ctx: Fly only, and the readout is age-related pathology: survival was never measured. No mammalian sensor-to-ageing evidence exists in this corpus.
edges.note: Added 2026-07-29. Gap H1 previously asserted the sensors link to ZERO ageing outcomes, which was true of the corpus but not of the literature.
edges.mech_beginner: The only case in this atlas linking a nutrient sensor to ageing of a whole animal: fruit flies without this sensor build up fat and develop muscle and heart problems, and blocking this pathway or switching on AMPK prevents it. So the sensor holds age-related damage back. Watch what was measured – how sick the flies got, not how long they lived.
edges.teach: The arrow now lands on Age-related pathology rather than on Longevity, because that is what LEE2010 measured: flies lacking Sestrin accumulate fat and develop muscle and cardiac pathology, and no lifespan was recorded. Sestrin holds that pathology back, which is why the sign is inhibits. It is the sensor arm's only organismal readout and it is not evidence that Sestrin2 extends life.

edges.mech: When leucine is scarce, free Sestrin2 clamps onto GATOR2 and blocks it, keeping the whole pathway switched off.
edges.mech_beginner: When there's no leucine, Sestrin2 grabs onto GATOR2 and holds the whole growth pathway shut.

edges.mech: SIN1 holds the complex together and positions the substrate; without it mTORC2 cannot phosphorylate Akt.
edges.mech_beginner: SIN1 holds mTORC2 together and positions its target – without it, mTORC2 can't switch Akt on.

edges.mech: SLC38A9 sits in the lysosomal membrane and reads arginine on the inside. Arginine-bound SLC38A9 acts as an exchange factor that loads RagA with GTP, switching the Rag dimer on (SHE2018B); it also pumps essential amino acids, including leucine, back out into the cytosol.
edges.note: Five independent studies - one of the best-supported edges in the sensor branch.
edges.mech_beginner: SLC38A9 sits in the lysosome's wall, senses arginine inside, and then flips RagA into its "on" shape, telling the Rag proteins there's enough.

edges.mech: SREBP1 is the main transcriptional switch for de novo lipogenesis, and SREBP2 for cholesterol synthesis.
edges.mech_beginner: SREBP is the master switch for making new fat from scratch.

edges.mech: AMPK does not read ATP directly - it reads the ratio of AMP and ADP to ATP. As ATP is consumed, AMP and ADP accumulate and bind the gamma subunit, which is the actual switch: it activates AMPK allosterically and protects the activating Thr172 phosphate from removal. AMPK is the cell's low-fuel sensor, and mTORC1 is one of the first things it shuts off.
edges.ctx: SOURCING FLAG (2026-09-29): the AMP/ADP binding to the gamma subunit described here is canonical, but no study currently in this corpus demonstrates it; GWI2008 and ZHO2001 show the downstream consequences. Treat as an unsourced canonical step until a primary paper is added.
edges.mech_beginner: When the cell's fuel runs low, AMPK switches on – it's the cell's low-battery alarm, and one of the first things it does is shut mTORC1 off.
edges.context: Drawn as a fuel-gauge for readability. The proximal trigger is the AMP(ADP)/ATP ratio binding the AMPK gamma subunit, not 'ATP running down' as a single variable - AMP and ADP both compete with ATP for the same regulatory sites.

edges.mech: Many different stresses do the same physical thing: they drag TSC2 onto the lysosome, right where Rheb is. That relocation, not a change in TSC2 amount, is the switch.
edges.note: Nice parallel to RAG-MTORC1 in the amino-acid route: both branches work by moving a protein to the lysosome.
edges.mech_beginner: Different kinds of stress all do the same physical thing: they drag TSC2 over to the lysosome, right next to Rheb. Moving it there is the switch, not making more of it.
edges.teach: Regulation by relocation: energy stress moves the TSC complex to the lysosome, where Rheb is. Location is a form of control the pathway uses repeatedly.

edges.mech: TBC1D7 is the third, often-forgotten subunit of the TSC complex; losing it weakens the brake without removing it.
edges.mech_beginner: TBC1D7 is a smaller, easy-to-miss third piece of the TSC brake; losing it weakens the brake without removing it.

edges.mech: Temsirolimus is the intravenous rapamycin analogue, and, to our knowledge, the first mTOR inhibitor to show an overall-survival benefit in a randomised trial.
edges.mech_beginner: Temsirolimus is the IV version of rapamycin, and the first mTOR-blocking drug shown to help patients live longer in a controlled trial.

edges.mech: In poor-prognosis renal cancer, temsirolimus improved overall survival against interferon - the hardest endpoint there is.
edges.ctx: Poor-prognosis patients specifically; the combination arm did not beat temsirolimus alone.
edges.note: Overall survival, not a surrogate. Worth pointing at.
edges.mech_beginner: In hard-to-treat kidney cancer, temsirolimus helped patients live longer compared with an older drug.

edges.mech: In the nucleus TFEB switches on a whole gene programme for autophagy and for building new lysosomes - the cell's recycling capacity, not just a single step.
edges.note: The transcriptional arm of autophagy, distinct from the fast ULK1 arm.
edges.mech_beginner: Once inside the nucleus, TFEB switches on a whole set of genes for cleanup and for building new lysosomes.
edges.context: Same flux caveat as ULK1-AUTOPHAGY: TFEB target-gene induction (more lysosomes, more autophagy machinery transcribed) is not itself proof that degradative flux increased - it raises capacity, which still needs to be confirmed with a flux readout rather than assumed from expression alone.

edges.mech: Sustained cap-dependent translation is what physically builds muscle. Blocking mTOR in humans blunts the protein-synthesis response to exercise.
edges.ctx: DRU2009 is direct human evidence: rapamycin blocked the contraction-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis in volunteers.
edges.note: Rare non-molecular badge in the output branch - DRU2009 is H, a human study.
edges.mech_beginner: Ongoing protein-building is what physically builds muscle – and in people, blocking mTOR blunts the rise in muscle protein-building after a single bout of exercise. That is the measurement that exists; how much muscle is gained over months under the drug was not measured.
edges.context: Requires mechanical load. mTORC1 activation without loading does not reproduce healthy hypertrophy, and constitutive activation alone is not sufficient.

edges.mech: The TSC complex is the pathway's main tumour suppressor. Inherit one broken copy and lesions grow wherever the second copy is lost - the clearest human evidence that mTORC1 activity drives tissue overgrowth.
edges.note: This is the edge that turns the biochemistry into a disease.
edges.mech_beginner: The TSC brake is the pathway's main tumour-suppressor. Inherit one broken copy of the gene and growths appear wherever the second copy is also lost. (This arrow skips a step for simplicity – TSC actually acts through Rheb first.)
edges.teach: A deliberate shortcut edge: TSC never touches mTORC1. It acts on Rheb. Shown so the overview reads cleanly; switch to Research level to see the two-step version.
edges.context: Deliberately compressed: TSC acts on Rheb, never on mTORC1. Kept as one link so the overview reads cleanly.

edges.mech: TSC2 is a GAP for Rheb: it forces Rheb to hydrolyse its GTP, switching it off. This is the single step where the tumour-suppressor function lives.
edges.mech_beginner: TSC2 forces Rheb to switch itself off – the one step where TSC acts as a tumour-suppressing brake.

edges.mech: ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK back, damping the signal that activated it - a negative feedback loop that stops autophagy running away.
edges.mech_beginner: ULK1 tags AMPK back and calms it down – a feedback loop that keeps cleanup from running out of control.
edges.teach: Closes the loop. ULK1 dampens the very kinase that activated it, so 'AMPK switches on autophagy' is a loop, not an arrow.
edges.context: Closes a loop rather than acting as a one-way arrow; steady-state behaviour depends on the relative strength of both directions.

edges.mech: Freed ULK1 nucleates the autophagosome - the self-eating programme that recycles damaged parts and is the leading candidate mechanism for mTOR inhibition's benefits.
edges.mech_beginner: Freed ULK1 kicks off autophagy – the cell's recycling programme, and the leading idea for why blocking this pathway might be beneficial.
edges.context: LC3-II accumulation, the standard readout for this step, marks autophagosome number, not flux: it rises whether autophagosomes are being made faster or degraded slower (e.g. under lysosomal/fusion block), so it cannot alone distinguish increased autophagy from stalled autophagy. A flux assay (e.g. LC3-II with and without a degradation blocker, or p62 turnover) is needed to tell the two apart.

edges.mech: The lysosome's proton pump talks to Ragulator from the inside out: amino acids inside the lysosome change v-ATPase, which changes Ragulator, which changes the Rags.
edges.ctx: The 'inside-out' model requires amino acids to accumulate inside the lysosome first; how they get there for every amino acid is not fully mapped.
edges.mech_beginner: The lysosome's acid pump senses amino acids from the inside and passes that information out to Ragulator, which passes it on to the Rag proteins.

edges.mech: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 only as a complex with FKBP12: the pair docks on the FRB domain beside the active site and blocks some substrates but not all, so S6K1 phosphorylation collapses while much of 4E-BP1 phosphorylation persists.
edges.ctx: Directness is graded indirect because the mechanism requires FKBP12, as for everolimus and the bi-sterics. Acute effect only; the chronic effect on mTORC2 is the separate RAPA-MTORC2 edge.
edges.mech_beginner: Rapamycin, carried by its helper protein FKBP12, jams part of mTORC1 – it blocks some of what mTORC1 does but not all of it.
edges.teach: Drawn as the functional arrow so that the map assigns the inhibition to the drug rather than to FKBP12. The physical route is RAPA-FKBP12 then FKBP12-MTORC1 (binding); FKBP12 without rapamycin does not inhibit mTORC1.

edges.mech: A second and contested way in: JEW2015 reports that glutamine activates mTORC1 without the Rag GTPases, through Arf1, and that leucine and glutamine therefore do not share one entry point. If it holds, Rag-dependent lysosomal recruitment is not the only route to the kinase.
edges.ctx: Cell-type dependent and not uniformly reproduced across labs. The Rag-dependent route is the separate GLN-RAG edge; neither edge should be read as covering the other.
edges.mech_beginner: Some experiments say glutamine has a second way in that skips the Rag proteins entirely. If that is right, the lysosome story is not the whole story – which is a big claim resting on thin evidence.
edges.teach: Kept separate from the Rag-dependent glutaminolysis edge on purpose. Weight of a claim and strength of its evidence are independent: this one would revise the architecture of the whole nutrient arm, and it rests on a single study in this corpus.

edges.mech: Mechanical loading raises mTORC1 signalling in skeletal muscle. Rapamycin given to human volunteers blocks the contraction-induced increase in muscle protein synthesis, placing mTORC1 causally between the load and the response.
edges.ctx: Compressed: load reaches mTORC1 through several routes, only some of which need IGF-1, and the map draws one arrow. The human evidence establishes that mTORC1 is required, not which upstream route carries the signal.
edges.teach: This is the rare case where the interruption experiment was done in people rather than inferred from cells. Human relevance is established here, not merely plausible – which is true of almost nothing else upstream in this map.

edges.mech: Reduced nutrient and energy availability lowers mTORC1 signalling through the amino-acid and energy arms simultaneously – the sensors detect scarcity, and AMPK detects the falling energy charge.
edges.ctx: Supporting evidence here is thinner than the claim's reputation. ROM2016 (two-year caloric restriction is tolerable in non-obese humans) and MAT2017 (rhesus survival) were removed as support in the 2026-09-21 audit because neither measured mTORC1; they belong to the CR-LONGEVITY edge, not to this one. SOL2014 found macronutrient RATIO mattered more than total intake in mice, so 'caloric restriction' may be the wrong variable name.
edges.teach: Fasting and caloric restriction are the oldest way to lower mTORC1 in a whole animal and the least mechanistically resolved: nobody can say which arm carries most of the effect in a given tissue, and the effect on mTORC1 itself varies between tissues.

edges.mech: Caloric restriction improved health and survival in rhesus monkeys, and macronutrient composition altered lifespan in mice.
edges.ctx: No human lifespan data exists. Effect direction is reproducible across several species; effect size and even the responsible variable (calories versus composition) are not settled.
edges.teach: Read the species line before the claim. Primate survival data is the closest thing to human evidence here, and it is still not human – and the two large rhesus studies famously disagreed on lifespan depending on the control diet.

edges.mech: Occupies the mTOR active site in competition with ATP, so inhibition does not depend on obstructing substrate access and is not partial in the way rapalog inhibition is.
edges.ctx: Cell-line pharmacology. Clinical development of this class has been limited by toxicity attributed to simultaneous mTORC2 inhibition, which is precisely what the bi-steric design tries to avoid.
edges.teach: The comparison between this and rapamycin is what exposed rapamycin-resistant outputs. Torin was built as a ruler, and what it measured was how much of mTORC1 rapamycin had been leaving alone.

edges.mech: The same active site is present in both complexes, so an ATP-competitive inhibitor cannot distinguish them.
edges.ctx: Explains the metabolic and immunological toxicity of this class relative to rapalogs; the magnitude in patients is not established from these cell-line studies.
edges.teach: Selectivity in this pathway comes from accessory subunits, not from the catalytic site – so a drug aimed at the site inherits no selectivity. That is a structural fact, not a design oversight.

edges.mech: A bivalent molecule engages an FKBP12-dependent site and the active site simultaneously, producing deeper mTORC1 inhibition than a rapalog while sparing mTORC2.
edges.ctx: Phase 1 in advanced solid tumours – a safety and pharmacodynamic result, not an efficacy verdict. Directness is graded indirect because, like rapalogs, the mechanism requires FKBP12. Consensus is emerging: one trial, newest evidence in the corpus.
edges.teach: This is what forty years of mechanism bought: a drug designed against a specific known weakness of the previous drug. The 4E-BP1 escape identified in cells in 2009 is the thing this molecule exists to close.

edges.mech: Nuclear TFEB switches on the lysosomal and autophagy gene programme as a single coordinated module, expanding the lysosomal compartment.
edges.ctx: Transcriptional output measured as gene expression and lysosomal markers; how much the compartment actually expands varies with cell type and starvation depth.
edges.mech_beginner: In the nucleus, TFEB switches on a whole gene package for cleanup and for building new lysosomes.
edges.teach: This is the arm that makes the pathway circular. mTORC1 controls TFEB, TFEB controls how many lysosomes exist, and lysosomes are where mTORC1 is controlled.

edges.mech: A larger, renewed lysosomal compartment changes the platform on which mTORC1 is regulated – the return leg of the lysosome-to-nucleus circuit.
edges.ctx: SET2012 establishes lysosome-to-nucleus signalling via mTOR and TFEB; the quantitative effect of compartment size on mTORC1 output is not resolved.
edges.mech_beginner: More, fresher lysosomes change the very platform that controls mTORC1 – closing a loop back to where the signal started.
edges.teach: Closing this arm turns a dangling output into a real feedback loop. Before it was curated, the map could not show that mTORC1 shapes its own regulatory surface.

edges.mech: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify at least two parallel relays carrying mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1: AMPK, and the heme-regulated inhibitor HRI acting through the integrated stress response.
edges.ctx: CRISPR screening in cell lines; the relative weight of the AMPK and HRI arms in tissue is untested.
edges.mech_beginner: When mitochondria – the cell's power plants – are damaged, at least two separate alarm signals reach mTORC1 to shut it down.
edges.teach: Multitiered by design. The cell does not read mitochondrial failure through one channel, which is why single-gene knockouts rarely abolish the response.

edges.mech: mTORC1 raises mitochondrial respiratory capacity through a YY1–PGC-1α transcriptional programme and through 4E-BP-dependent translation of respiratory components.
edges.ctx: Effect size varies strongly by tissue; the transcriptional and translational arms have not been cleanly separated in vivo. OVERLAP (audit 2026-09-04): this edge and MTORC1-MITO assert overlapping biology from overlapping citations (CUN2007, MOR2013) at different tiers and different consensus levels. Read them together; they are not independent support.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 boosts how much energy mitochondria can produce, through both gene activation and protein-building. One mouse experiment points the other way – removing mTORC1 from fat tissue RAISED respiration – so this direction is not settled in a living animal.
edges.teach: One of the few places mTORC1 acts mainly through transcription – and one where a genetic experiment points the other way. Adipose Raptor knockout, which REMOVES mTORC1, produced lean mice with enhanced mitochondrial respiration (POL2008). That result is carried as conflicting evidence; it was previously cited here as genetic confirmation, which inverted its sign (audit 2026-09-21).

edges.mech: mTOR interacts with YY1 and is required for the YY1–PGC-1α complex to drive mitochondrial gene expression; rapamycin lowers both the transcripts and oxygen consumption.
edges.ctx: Single-study support in this corpus for the direct interaction; the downstream respiratory phenotype is better replicated than the binding itself.
edges.mech_beginner: mTOR works together with a gene-activating team to switch on mitochondrial genes – a rare example of this pathway acting inside the nucleus rather than at the cell's outer edges. The direct interaction rests on a single study in this Atlas.
edges.teach: A nuclear action of a kinase usually taught as cytosolic. The pathway is not confined to the lysosomal surface and the cytosol.

edges.mech: Unleashing mTORC1 by deleting TSC1 drives quiescent haematopoietic stem cells into cycle, raises mitochondrial biogenesis and floods them with ROS; an antioxidant rescues self-renewal.
edges.ctx: Demonstrated in haematopoietic stem cells, where quiescence is the baseline state. Cell types that are already cycling need not behave this way.
edges.mech_beginner: Switching mTORC1 on too much pushes resting stem cells to start dividing and floods them with reactive, damaging molecules; giving them antioxidants restores their normal function.
edges.teach: The antioxidant rescue is what makes this causal rather than correlative – ROS is the mediator, not a side observation.

edges.mech: Oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K–Akt–mTORC1–eIF4A cascade that selectively promotes cap-dependent translation of P-glycoprotein.
edges.ctx: One cell-line study in a multidrug-resistance context; whether the loop runs in normal physiology at these ROS levels is untested.
edges.mech_beginner: Oxidative damage can itself switch on mTORC1 through a chain of signals, closing a feedback loop that can turn a brief stress into a lasting one.
edges.teach: Together with mTORC1 → ROS this would close a positive feedback loop, which would amplify rather than stabilise a transient oxidative insult. The two arms come from different systems (haematopoietic stem cells in mice, a multidrug-resistant cell line), so the loop is a hypothesis assembled from two papers, not a measured circuit.

edges.mech: mTORC2–Akt signalling localises to mitochondria-associated ER membranes and regulates mitochondrial physiology from there.
edges.ctx: Biochemical fractionation and imaging in cell lines; the functional contribution relative to plasma-membrane mTORC2 is not quantified.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC2 signalling also happens at a specific contact point between mitochondria and another cell structure – proof this pathway works at more than one location in the cell.
edges.teach: Direct evidence that mTOR signalling happens at more than one membrane. The lysosome is where mTORC1 is switched on; it is not the only place mTOR works.

edges.mech: Akt phosphorylates FOXO transcription factors and excludes them from the nucleus. Rictor or mLST8 deletion abolishes signalling to Akt–FOXO while sparing S6K1.
edges.ctx: Mouse knockouts and cell lines; FOXO isoform contributions differ by tissue.
edges.mech_beginner: Akt tags FOXO proteins and keeps them out of the nucleus; this specific link belongs to mTORC2, not mTORC1.
edges.teach: The clean genetic separation: this arm belongs to mTORC2, not mTORC1. It also means rapamycin does not release FOXO the way an mTOR kinase inhibitor can.

edges.mech: TOR signalling and rapamycin influence lifespan partly through the SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO transcriptional programmes.
edges.ctx: C. elegans only. DAF-16 is the FOXO orthologue; mapping worm lifespan genetics onto mammalian FOXO1/3 is an inference, not a demonstration.
edges.mech_beginner: Part of how this pathway affects lifespan runs through stress-resistance genes switched on by FOXO – so far shown mainly in simple animals like worms, not yet in mammals.
edges.teach: An invertebrate result. It is the mechanistic basis most often cited for 'mTOR inhibition acts through stress-resistance programmes', and it has not been shown in mammals in this corpus.

edges.mech: mTOR inhibition reverses Akt-driven prostate intraepithelial neoplasia partly through HIF-1-dependent pathways, placing HIF-1α downstream of mTORC1 in this setting.
edges.ctx: Mouse prostate model with pharmacological mTOR inhibition; HIF-1α is one of several pathways implicated in the same experiment.
edges.mech_beginner: In one specific setting (prostate cells), mTORC1 turns on a factor usually associated with low oxygen – here it's mTORC1 driving it, not the other way around.
edges.teach: Note the direction. Hypoxia → HIF-1α is the arm everyone expects, but it is mTORC1 → HIF-1α that this corpus supports; the hypoxia arm is drawn here through REDD1 instead, because that is what the cited paper shows.

edges.mech: Age-related decline of the Ragulator subunit Lamtor5 impairs mTORC1 signalling in macrophages, and this loss of restraint is sufficient to unleash cGAS-mediated paracrine inflammatory signalling; restoring Lamtor5 in aged mice reverses the phenotype.
edges.ctx: One mouse study (LV2026), A – animal. Exactly how reduced mTORC1 output in a macrophage permits cGAS activation is not resolved here, and no human data exist for this specific link.
edges.teach: The sign here is a brake being released, not a switch being thrown: Ragulator/Lamtor5 does not touch cGAS or STING directly, it maintains an mTORC1 signalling state that keeps the sensor pathway quiet. Ageing removes the brake.

edges.mech: cGAS-STING activation in aged macrophages drives a paracrine inflammatory senescence programme that spreads the phenotype to neighbouring cells, contributing to systemic ageing.
edges.ctx: Single mouse study; the human magnitude of this effect, and whether the same paracrine spread occurs in human tissue, are untested.
edges.teach: 'Paracrine' is the operative word: senescence signalling propagates outward from the affected macrophages to other cells rather than staying cell-autonomous – part of why restoring Lamtor5 in one compartment produced a systemic phenotype reversal.

edges.mech: Malonyl-CoA, an intermediate of fatty-acid synthesis, binds directly into the mTOR kinase's ATP-binding catalytic pocket and competes with ATP, switching mTORC1 down when fatty-acid synthesis is impaired and malonyl-CoA accumulates.

ERK2 directly phosphorylates the purine-making enzyme PFAS within minutes, speeding de novo purine synthesis. This growth signal for DNA and RNA building blocks runs in parallel to mTORC1's own routes.
edges.ctx: Human cancer cell lines and xenograft tumours; ERK2, not ERK1; post-translational and parallel to mTORC1. Single study.
edges.mech_beginner: ERK2 switches on an enzyme that makes purines.

edges.mech: Growth hormone / IGF-1 signalling acts as a brake on lifespan: mice whose GH signalling is blocked, either lifelong or from middle age, live longer and are less frail in old age.
edges.ctx: Mouse only. A lifelong GH-receptor-antagonist transgenic (LIST2026; an earlier study of the same line did not detect extension) and a tamoxifen-inducible whole-body Ghr knockout started at 12 months (DUR2026). mTOR signalling was not measured in either, so the route through PI3K-Akt-mTOR is inferred, not shown here.
edges.mech_beginner: Less growth-hormone signalling, longer life in mice.

edges.mech: Active mTORC1, acting through the transcription factor c-MYC, raises production of MAT2A, the enzyme that makes SAM, so a growing cell makes more of its main methyl donor.
edges.ctx: Human cell lines and mouse xenograft tumours; acts through c-MYC on MAT2A. Together with SAM-SAMTOR this forms a loop whose behaviour in normal tissue is untested. Single study.
edges.mech_beginner: mTORC1 tells the cell to make more SAM.

edges.mech: PDCD4 binds the mTORC2 subunit Rictor through three basic residues, which stops mTORC2 from assembling properly and lowers its kinase activity.
edges.ctx: Human NSCLC cell lines and mouse xenografts; not shown in normal tissue. Single study.
edges.mech_beginner: PDCD4 grabs Rictor and keeps mTORC2 from working.

edges.mech: When amino acids run out, the Rag GTPases also pull the TSC complex onto the lysosome, where it can switch Rheb off and help shut mTORC1 down.
edges.ctx: Mammalian cell lines under acute amino-acid withdrawal; the contribution of this route in tissues is not established. Single study.
edges.mech_beginner: Without amino acids, the Rags bring the TSC brake to the lysosome.

edges.mech: When lysosomes are stressed, ULK1 (or its relative TBK1) phosphorylates FNIP1 at S296 on the lysosome. This switches the FLCN-FNIP complex off, so mTORC1 can no longer hold TFEB in the cytoplasm and TFEB moves into the nucleus.
edges.ctx: Human cell lines and ATP6V1B2-mutant follicular lymphoma samples; a nutrient-independent lysosomal-stress route, and TBK1 can substitute for ULK1. Single study.
edges.mech_beginner: ULK1 tags FNIP1, which turns FLCN off and lets TFEB escape mTORC1's grip.
